 El-Sayed says Israel should not identify with a faith, pushes back on antisemitism concerns
 The Michigan senator-elect argued that Jewish Americans should distinguish between their safety and discomfort over criticism of Israel
 Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images
 Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed poses for a portrait in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on Saturday, Feb. 21, 2026.
 By 
 AJ Rodriguez 
 November 18, 2026 
 SHARE Share options Facebook 
 Telegram 
 LinkedIn 
 WhatsApp 
 Reddit 
 Add JewishInsider on Google 
 Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) said Tuesday that Israel should not identify itself with a particular religion or culture, while pushing back against concerns that his criticism of the Jewish state contributes to fears of antisemitism among Jewish Americans.
 Speaking at The Atlantic Summit: Politics, Power, and What’s Next in Washington, El-Sayed argued that Israel should guarantee equal rights to all its citizens without defining its national identity through religion or culture, raising further questions about his support for Israel’s existence as a Jewish state.
 “I believe that Israel ought to be a country that upholds equal rights for all of its citizens, does not identify itself with a culture or a faith, and that dignifies the rights of those citizens to live free under its laws,” El-Sayed told Atlantic staff writer Jonathan Lemire.
 The Michigan Democrat also declined to endorse a specific framework for resolving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, arguing that Palestinians and Jewish Israelis should negotiate their political future on equal terms rather than have a settlement imposed on them.
 Israel should not “identify with a culture or a faith,” Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said at The Atlantic Summit, a new iteration of his belief that Israel should not exist as a Jewish state.
AJ Rodriguez reports: https://t.co/Hdv4D1BJbv pic.twitter.com/udtAkH0wMp 
— Jewish Insider (@jewishinsider) November 18, 2026 
 El-Sayed said the eventual arrangement could involve one state, two states or another configuration, maintaining that the decision should be made by the two populations rather than American policymakers.
 Asked how he would respond to someone who said his criticism of Israel fueled fears of antisemitism, El-Sayed acknowledged those concerns but argued that personal discomfort over his political positions should not be confused with threats to safety.
 “I’m sorry for your fear. Obviously, I don’t want to do anything that drives your fear,” El-Sayed said. “At the end of the day, there’s a difference between safety or lack of safety and comfort.”
 El-Sayed went on to argue that criticism of Israel’s prosecution of the war in Gaza in Gaza should not be suppressed because it makes some people uncomfortable, saying that those disturbed by his rhetoric should also be concerned about Palestinian suffering.
 The senator-elect also accused the United States of enabling what he called a genocide in Gaza and demanded accountability from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he accused of committing war crimes.
 His latest remarks follow months of controversy over his positions on Israel and antisemitism, including his repeated reluctance to affirm Israel’s right to exist without qualifications.
 Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said at yesterday’s The Atlantic Summit that those concerned his rhetoric on Israel fuels antisemitism “should be uncomfortable with injustice perpetrated on another people,” but added that he does not want to “make anybody unsafe.” pic.twitter.com/MfqWkCgsEn 
— Jewish Insider (@jewishinsider) November 18, 2026 
 In a November interview with CBS’ “60 Minutes ,” El-Sayed conditioned his support for Israel’s existence on an agreement between Palestinians and Israelis over their political future. He said he would support either a two-state solution or a single shared state if both populations agreed.
 During the campaign, a coalition of Michigan Jewish leaders pressed El-Sayed to affirm Jewish sovereignty in Israel and more directly address antisemitism motivated by hostility toward the Jewish state. El-Sayed maintained that he was committed to protecting Jewish Americans, but several Democratic Jewish leaders said his assurances failed to address their concerns.
